---
title: Containerization
description: Containerize your seedcord bots and use them as images, for development or production.
---

In order to containerize your application, you'll need the following prerequisites:

- Your .env file
- Docker Engine
- Access to Docker Hub (or the container registry you'd like to pull images from)
- Dev Containers also need a dev container runner (such as VS Code via the [Dev Container](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=ms-vscode-remote.remote-containers) extension)

## Containerizing for production

To containerize your application, you'll need to write a Dockerfile and, optionally, a Docker Compose file.

To write a Dockerfile, first pull the image(s) you want, then perform copying and building steps within that image. We recommend using slim images for faster pull times, smaller output, and reduced attack surfaces.

Here's an example Dockerfile (and .dockerignore) to get you started:

```gitignore title=.dockerignore
node_modules
dist
# almost literally every dotfolder is not needed and can be excluded for maximum layer caching
**/.*
# If you use build-time environment variables, uncomment the line below:
# !.env

# add other files that you don't need to include in your image if you want to optimize caching
```

```Dockerfile title=Dockerfile
# Use the official Node.js image from Docker Hub
# Replace :lts-slim with the slimmed version you want to use, example: ":24-slim"
FROM node:lts-slim
# Or use something that can manage your Node runtime, like:
# Vite+: FROM ghcr.io/voidzero-dev/vite-plus:latest
# pnpm: FROM ghcr.io/pnpm/pnpm:latest

# For the sake of organization, we'll use a workdir.
WORKDIR /app

# For a repo using pnpm, install pnpm in some way here (same idea for yarn)
# Some images may already have pnpm or automatically download it
RUN npm install -g pnpm

# Repeat this for as many package.jsons as you need to build your bot
COPY ./package.json ./

# Replace the lines below with your package manager's lockfile + any other relevant files
COPY ./pnpm-workspace.yaml ./
COPY ./pnpm-lock.yaml ./

RUN pnpm install --frozen-lockfile

COPY . .

# Run the build script
RUN pnpm run build

# Docker runs this command in the specified intervals to check the health of your bot
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --retries=3 --start-interval=5s --start-period=5s --timeout=30s \
    CMD ["node", "--input-type=module", "-e", "const response = await fetch('http://localhost:6967/health'); if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`)"]
    # Note that the bot starts at port 3000, and therefore its healthcheck server also lives on localhost:3000/health

# When this container is executed directly, it will run this command.
# Replace with the appropriate run command (shown to you after building)
CMD ["node", "--enable-source-maps", "dist/index.mjs"]
```

In your bot instance, make sure you set `lifecycle.shutdownDeadline` to ~5000, since Docker by default grants a container 10s to shutdown, which means that setting it to half leaves room for extra cleanup such as log flushing.

### Using a Docker Compose

If you want to use a Docker Compose file, create a file named `docker-compose.yml` with the contents of either of these:

```yml title=docker-compose.yml
# Use this for Gateway bots
services:
    gateway-bot:
        build:
            context: .
            dockerfile: ./Dockerfile
        container_name: discord-bot
        # Optionally expose healthcheck server for external healthchecking
        ports:
            - 6967:6967
        env_file: ./.env
        volumes:
            - ./logs:/app/logs
```

```yml title=docker-compose.yml
# Use this for HTTP bots
services:
    http-bot:
        build:
            context: .
            dockerfile: ./Dockerfile
        container_name: discord-bot
        # If using Docker Desktop, this requires host networking to be enabled
        # network_mode: 'host'
        # Or, you can also explicitly map ports via the ports: object, like so:
        ports:
            - 3000:3000
        env_file: ./.env
        volumes:
            - ./logs:/app/logs
```

This can be helpful for any non-trivial bot, such as for:

- Mounting a directory or volume into the container:

```yml title=docker-compose.yml
services:
    bot:
        build:
            context: .
            dockerfile: ./Dockerfile
        container_name: discord-bot
        env_file: ./.env
        volumes:
            - ./assets:/app/assets
            - ./logs:/app/logs
            - bot-data:/app/data
volumes:
    bot-data:
```

- Starting other services (e.g. a database) alongside your bot

```yml title=docker-compose.yml
services:
    bot:
        build:
            context: .
            dockerfile: ./Dockerfile
        container_name: discord-bot
        env_file: ./.env
        volumes:
            - ./logs:/app/logs
    postgres:
        image: postgres:latest
        container_name: discord-bot-db
        environment:
            - POSTGRES_PASSWORD=some-password-here
```

- Passing in runtime secrets or variables (with or without the use of `.env`)

```yml title=docker-compose.yml
services:
    bot:
        build:
            context: .
            dockerfile: ./Dockerfile
        container_name: discord-bot
        environment:
            DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN: ${DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN}
        # or, if you're brave, mount the `.env` file into the container
        volumes:
            - ./.env:/app/.env
            - ./logs:/app/logs
```

### Multi-stage container builds

When you want to reduce your overall iamge size, you may want to use multi-stage container builds to separate each stage.

When you want to do this, you'll need to define multiple stages:

```Dockerfile title=Dockerfile
FROM node:lts-slim AS build
# Or any other container with your dev tool

WORKDIR /app

# build steps go here

FROM node:lts-slim AS dependencies
# Or any other container with your dev tool
# This step is only needed if you externalise dependencies

WORKDIR /deps

# Install pnpm in some way here
# Some images may already have pnpm or automatically download it
RUN npm install -g pnpm

COPY package.json ./
COPY pnpm-lock.yaml ./
COPY pnpm-workspace.yaml ./

RUN pnpm install --production

FROM node:lts-slim AS runner
# Here, you wouldn't use the container with your dev tools, just your production runner image
# (i.e. use a slim Node.js image instead of e.x. Vite+ or pnpm images)

# Replace dist/ with the folder containing your bot
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist/
# Only needed if you included the dependencies stage
COPY --from=dependencies /deps/node_modules ./node_modules/

# Optional healthcheck
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --retries=3 --start-interval=5s --start-period=5s --timeout=30s \
    CMD ["node", "--input-type=module", "-e", "const response = await fetch('http://localhost:6967/health'); if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`)"]

CMD ["node", "--enable-source-maps", "dist/index.mjs"]
```

By default, seedcord requires your `dist` output, `package.json` and `node_modules`

## Configuring a dev container

The Dev Containers specification is made for development environments inside one or more containers. This is helpful for quickly developing and iterating with all the tools you need, no prerequisite installations required.

To set up a dev container environment for a seedcord project, you'll need to define a couple files:

```json title=.devcontainer/devcontainer.json
{
    // Open the bot service from the Docker Compose file below
    "dockerComposeFile": "../docker-compose.yml",
    "service": "bot",
    // Your editor opens the bot service's bind mount at this folder
    "workspaceFolder": "/app",
    // Instead of a Compose file, specify an image or build.dockerfile for direct usage of a Dockerfile, and drop the three keys above.
    // "image": "node:latest", // or any development image like pnpm or Vite+
    // build: { dockerfile: "./Dockerfile" }
    "postCreateCommand": "npm install", // optional
    "postStartCommand": "npm exec seedcord codegen" // optional
}
```

```yml title=docker-compose.yml
# Only needed if dockerComposeFile specified in devcontainer.json
services:
    bot:
        image: node:lts # or any dev image like pnpm or Vite+
        container_name: discord-bot-dev
        # Keep the container running so your editor can attach
        command: sleep infinity
        volumes:
            - .:/app:cached
    postgres: # Start a development PostgreSQL DB alongside your bot
        image: postgres:latest
        container_name: discord-bot-dev-postgres
        environment:
            - POSTGRES_PASSWORD=some-password-here
```

`node:24` exits as soon as it starts, and your editor attaches to a running container, so `sleep infinity` holds the `bot` service open. The `volumes` entry mounts your project at `/app`, which is the `workspaceFolder` your editor opens.

```Dockerfile title=Dockerfile
# Only needed if specified in either devcontainer.json or docker-compose.yml
FROM node:24
# or any development image like pnpm or Vite+

# Rest of steps should be similar to the container builds scenario above
```
